replacement: “Good Lord!” I thought. “At a moment like this he is thinking of other people’s respect!” I felt so sorry for him that I believe I would have shared his fate if that could have comforted him. I saw he was beside himself. I was horrified, for I understood with my heart as well as my mind what such a decision meant.

Then he took out all the things he had kept for fourteen years, which he thought would prove his crime, and laid them on the table. There were the murdered woman’s jewels, which he had stolen to turn suspicion away. There was a cross and a locket taken from her neck, with a portrait of her betrothed inside. There was her notebook, and two letters: one from her betrothed, telling her he would soon be with her, and her unfinished reply, left on the table to be sent next day. He had carried off those two letters—what for? Why had he kept them for fourteen years afterward, instead of destroying them as evidence against him?
